   949  Principle 5 demands that ``[t]he Federal work force should be used 
   950  efficiently and effectively,'' 5 U.S.C. 2301(b)(5), which means that 
   951  Federal agencies must be able to restructure efficiently in response to 
   952  evolving mission needs and the public interest. OPM has repeatedly 
   953  emphasized that agencies must be able to restructure efficiently to 
   954  align their workforces with changing missions, budget realities, 
   955  technology, and service-delivery needs.\6\
   956  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
   957  
   958      \5\ OPM, Human Capital Framework, https://www.opm.gov/policy-data-oversight/human-capital-framework/.
   959      \6\ See OPM, Implementing Reshaping Options, https://www.opm.gov/policy-data-oversight/workforce-restructuring/reshaping/implementing-reshaping-options/; OPM, Executive Playbook for 
   960  Workforce Reshaping, https://www.opm.gov/policy-data-oversight/workforce-restructuring/reshaping/accelerating-the-gears-of-transformation/executive-playbook-for-workforce-reshaping.pdf.
   961  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
   962  
   963      Commenter 0687 observed that ``the government should not presume

   970  sometimes necessary to reduce headcount in some areas while bolstering

   972      OPM believes that Federal agencies should be able to retain their

   975  people needed to carry out its statutory mission after the reduction is 
   976  complete. Thus, OPM agrees with Commenter 0687, who supports the

   982      Indeed, when an agency is reducing positions because of budget,

  1000  [[Page 49186]]
  1001  
  1002  performance a more central role in determining retention standing.
  1003      Federal agencies have confirmed that they would like greater 
  1004  ability to retain their highest-performing employees during a RIF. 
  1005  Commenter 0720, a Federal agency, stated that it ``would like to be 
  1006  able to retain its higher performing employees during RIF actions and 
  1007  this rule would enable it to do so.'' Commenter 0720 noted that OPM's 
  1008  proposed performance-weighted RIF framework ``offers a more accurate 
  1009  reflection of employee contributions and reduces the likelihood that 
  1010  restructuring disproportionately affects high performers.'' Under the 
  1011  current rules, performance affects retention standing only after tenure 
  1012  group and veterans' preference subgroup are applied, and only by being 
  1013  translated into additional years of service. As Commenter 0720 
  1014  observed: ``Under the current RIF rules an employee's performance 
  1015  functions primarily as a modest supplement to their seniority.'' OPM 
  1016  believes that this structure can cause higher-performing employees to 
  1017  be released ahead of lower-performing employees and that a more direct 
  1018  performance-credit system better promotes an efficient and effective 
  1019  civil service.
  1020      In OPM's view, current RIF rules are unnecessarily cumbersome, 
  1021  inflexible, intricate, time-consuming, and resource-intensive, and they 
  1022  can create unnecessary risk of implementation error. In the proposed 
  1023  rule, OPM cited a longtime Federal employee who described the current 
  1024  RIF rules and regulations as ``complex and cumbersome,'' creating a 
  1025  ``time-consuming and demoralizing process'' that leads to outcomes that 
  1026  are ``haphazard and invariably negative.'' Fred Mills, Civil 
  1027  Disservice: Federal Employment Culture and the Challenge of Genuine 
  1028  Reform, at p. 42 (iUniverse 2010). Commenter 0720 noted recent 
  1029  difficulties in implementing workforce reshaping that imposed 
  1030  unnecessary costs and burdens and contended that these difficulties 
  1031  ``provide compelling evidence of the need for the streamlined, 
  1032  modernized, and more administratively feasible framework proposed by 
  1033  OPM.'' Commenter 0720 states that OPM's reforms ``will simplify 
  1034  execution, reduce administrative errors, and increase consistency 
  1035  across agency components.''
  1036      Commenter 0685 noted that ``[a] central feature of the current 
  1037  [RIF] framework is its administrative complexity, which can 
  1038  significantly impede implementation.'' Commenter 0685 observed that 
  1039  ``[t]he procedural demands of the current system also contribute to 
  1040  significant delays in the execution of workforce restructuring 
  1041  decisions.'' Further, Commenter 0685 noted that the current framework 
  1042  imposes substantial resource costs on agencies. Implementing a RIF 
  1043  under existing rules often requires human resources specialists, legal 
  1044  counsel, and management personnel to dedicate significant time and 
  1045  effort to navigating procedural requirements. Commenter 0091, a Federal 
  1046  agency, noted that the current rules contribute to an existing 
  1047  ``critical weakness''; namely, the ``federal government's historic lack 
  1048  of agility in dynamic environments.''
  1049      Indeed, the current rules require agencies to classify employees by 
  1050  tenure group, veterans' preference subgroup, service computation date, 
  1051  and performance-adjusted service credit, and then apply additional 
  1052  rules governing release, assignment rights, bumping, retreating, 
  1053  notices, and related placement obligations. They increase the 
  1054  likelihood of error, impede timely restructuring, and make it more 
  1055  difficult for agencies to retain top performing employees in a RIF. OPM 
  1056  believes that a clearer register based on performance points, veterans' 
  1057  preference points, tenure subgroup, and actual SCD will be easier for 
  1058  agencies to apply and easier for employees to understand.
  1059      Commenter 0680 argued that the current regulations do not 
  1060  prioritize length of service over performance because performance 
  1061  credit and length of service are added together. OPM disagrees.
  1062      Under the current RIF rules, performance and length of service are 
  1063  combined only after tenure group and veterans' preference subgroup have 
  1064  already been applied. In addition, performance is capped through the 
  1065  current additional-service-credit formula, while actual service may 
  1066  continue to accumulate over an employee's career. That means current 
  1067  RIF ordering is not a simple comparison of Employee A's performance 
  1068  against Employee B's performance. Agencies must first place employees 
  1069  into tenure groups, then veterans' preference subgroups, then calculate 
  1070  adjusted service dates. Performance affects ranking only inside the 
  1071  employee's already-determined tenure/veterans' category. The current 
  1072  formula therefore does not give performance the same effect as this 
  1073  final rule does.
  1074      The current system therefore does not allow performance to overcome 
  1075  many of the most important retention categories. A high-performing 
  1076  employee in a lower tenure group cannot outrank a lower-performing 
  1077  employee in a higher tenure group; and within the same tenure group, 
  1078  performance cannot overcome veterans' preference subgroup placement. 
  1079  Performance matters only within the employee's already-determined group 
  1080  and subgroup. That means current performance credit is not a true 
  1081  performance-first retention rule; it is a service-date adjustment 
  1082  applied at the end of a categorical ranking system.
  1083      Even within the same tenure group and veterans' preference 
  1084  subgroup, the current system gives performance a relatively narrow 
  1085  practical effect. The difference between three Level 5 ratings and 
  1086  three Level 3 ratings is only 8 years of adjusted service credit: 20 
  1087  years versus 12 years. So a long-serving employee with three Fully 
  1088  Successful ratings can still outrank a much higher-performing employee 
  1089  with three Outstanding ratings if the long-serving employee has more 
  1090  than an 8-year service advantage. Current 5 CFR 351.504 requires the 
  1091  performance credits to be averaged, rounded, and expressed as 
  1092  additional years of service. Level 5 ratings add 20 years, Level 4 
  1093  ratings add 16 years, and Level 3 ratings add 12 years to the 
  1094  employee's retention-service credit.
  1095      For example, assume two employees are in the same tenure group and 
  1096  veterans' preference subgroup:
  1097  
  1098  --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  1099                   Employee                    Actual SCD        Ratings      Current performance credit   Adjusted SCD         Current rule  outcome
  1100  --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  1101  Employee A...............................            1996           3/3/3  +12 years..................            1984  Ranks higher.
  1102  Employee B...............................            2021           5/5/5  +20 years..................            2001  Ranks lower.
  1103  --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  1104  
  1105      Employee B is clearly the higher performer, but Employee A is 
  1106  retained because Employee A's longer service overwhelms the 8-year 
  1107  performance differential. That illustrates the core problem: the 
  1108  current system does not really prioritize performance but merely gives 
  1109  performance a modest service-date boost.
  1110  
  1111  [[Page 49187]]
  1112  
  1113      The current method is also opaque. It requires agencies and 
  1114  employees to translate ratings into artificial years of service, 
  1115  average those values, round them, subtract them from the employee's 
  1116  actual SCD, and then rank employees by the resulting adjusted SCD. That 
  1117  makes performance harder to see and harder to explain because the final 
  1118  ranking appears as a date rather than as a performance score.
  1119      The approach in this final rule is more transparent. Performance 
  1120  remains performance, measured in points. Length of service remains 
  1121  length of service, measured by actual SCD. OPM reasonably concluded 
  1122  that this system is easier to administer and easier for employees to 
  1123  understand than a performance-adjusted SCD. These regulations still 
  1124  give length of service effect as a tie-breaker when employees have the 
  1125  same augmented performance credit and tenure subgroup.
  1126      The direct point system that OPM adopts in this rule better 
  1127  advances the goal of a merit-based workforce because it makes 
  1128  performance a central, visible, and auditable factor in determining 
  1129  retention standing. Under these regulations, agencies will assign 
  1130  direct point values to ratings (Level 5 = 7 points, Level 4 = 5 points, 
  1131  Level 3 = 3 points, and Level 1 or 2 = 0 points) and then sum the 
  1132  values for the employee's three most recent ratings. Employees will 
  1133  then be ranked within the same tenure group by performance credit as 
  1134  augmented by veterans' preference points; only if employees tie would 
  1135  the agency use tenure subgroup and then actual SCD.
  1136      Using the same example under the proposed rule:
  1137  
  1138  ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  1139                                                                  Proposed
  1140                    Employee                       Ratings       performance                  Result
  1141                                                                   credit
  1142  ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  1143  Employee A.................................           3/3/3               9  Ranks lower.
  1144  Employee B.................................           5/5/5              21  Ranks higher.
  1145  ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  1146  
  1147      That outcome better reflects merit. The employee with three 
  1148  Outstanding ratings outranks the employee with three Fully Successful 
  1149  ratings, regardless of the fact that the lower-performing employee has 
  1150  longer service. Length of service is still considered, but only as a 
  1151  tie-breaker after performance credit, veterans' preference, and tenure 
  1152  subgroup have been applied.
  1153      In short, the current system gives performance nominal credit but 
  1154  not meaningful priority. It buries performance inside seniority, lets 
  1155  long service overwhelm even large performance differences, and prevents 
  1156  performance from crossing tenure and veterans' preference subgroup 
  1157  boundaries. This final rule makes performance visible, direct, 
  1158  auditable, and outcome-affecting, while still preserving veterans' 
  1159  preference, tenure, and length of service in the retention framework.
  1160  
  1161  F. The Final Rule Reasonably Balances Retention of Institutional 
  1162  Knowledge With Retention of High Performers
  1163  
  1164      Commenter 0672 argued that the rule may harm recruitment, 
  1165  retention, and institutional knowledge. OPM acknowledges that length of 
  1166  service and institutional knowledge are important. However, OPM 
  1167  believes that the current system overvalues tenure at the expense of 
  1168  performance. This final rule does not eliminate length of service; it 
  1169  uses length of service as the final tie-breaker after performance 
  1170  credit, veterans' preference, and tenure subgroup are considered. OPM 
  1171  has reasonably determined that the public interest is better served by 
  1172  a RIF system that allows agencies to retain employees with the 
  1173  strongest demonstrated performance while still recognizing tenure, 
  1174  veterans' preference, and service.
  1175      Long service may reflect valuable experience. But performance 
  1176  ratings are a more direct measure of how well an employee is 
  1177  contributing to agency mission needs than seniority alone. As Commenter 
  1178  0720, a Federal agency, noted: ``Where more senior employees have 
  1179  gained experience that makes them more effective in advancing the 
  1180  agency's mission this greater effectiveness is typically reflected in 
  1181  their performance ratings.'' Thus, Commenter 0720 stated that ``it 
  1182  makes more sense for the RIF regulations to target retaining high 
  1183  performers directly, by prioritizing performing as a retention 
  1184  criterion, than indirectly through seniority,'' as in its experience, 
  1185  ``employee performance ratings are more strongly correlated with their 
  1186  performance and effectiveness than pure seniority.''
  1187      Commenter 0686, another Federal agency, noted that prioritizing 
  1188  performance over tenure and length of service ``ensures top 
  1189  performance, regardless of tenure, continues to be prioritized for 
  1190  retention decisions. This revision acknowledges that tenure is not 
  1191  always a reflection of an employee's knowledge or capabilities'' and 
  1192  ``ensures that merit-based performance takes precedence over seniority, 
  1193  which is a more effective way to retain skilled and high-performing 
  1194  staff.''
  1195      OPM agrees with Commenters 0720 and 0686 that a RIF system that 
  1196  retains higher performers better serves the public and better supports 
  1197  agency operations after restructuring--and that high performance is 
  1198  more accurately measured through performance ratings, not pure 
  1199  seniority. OPM rejects Commenter 0653's assertion that performance 
  1200  appraisals cannot capture the value of institutional knowledge; 
  1201  instead, OPM believes that institutional knowledge that meaningfully 
  1202  advances agency missions will be appropriately reflected in performance 
  1203  ratings of record issued under 5 U.S.C. 4302.
  1204      OPM agrees that agencies must protect mission delivery during and 
  1205  after a RIF but disagrees that a tenure-first system is the best way to 
  1206  do so. A RIF leaves an agency with fewer employees, making it 
  1207  especially important that the employees retained are those with the 
  1208  strongest demonstrated ability to perform the agency's evolving 
  1209  mission-critical work.
  1210      OPM rejects Commenter 0532's characterization that the proposal 
  1211  assumes longer-serving employees are poor performers. The rule does not 
  1212  rest on any such assumption. It simply recognizes that length of 
  1213  service and performance are distinct statutory factors, and that a 
  1214  modern RIF system should give greater weight to demonstrated 
  1215  performance when agencies must make difficult retention decisions.
  1216      A merit-based RIF system should not operate solely based on how 
  1217  long employees have served or on the formal category into which they 
  1218  fall. It should also reflect demonstrated performance and the 
  1219  government's need to retain an effective workforce during 
  1220  restructuring. Congress made performance one of the statutory RIF 
  1221  factors, and this rule gives that factor more transparent and 
  1222  meaningful effect.
  1223  
  1224  [[Page 49188]]
  1225  
  1226  G. The Size of Recent Workforce Reductions Does Not Undermine the Basis 
  1227  for the Rule
  1228  
  1229      Commenters 0532, 0320, and 0616 contended that, because the 
  1230  Government was able to reduce the workforce under existing rules, OPM 
  1231  cannot claim the current RIF rules are burdensome. OPM disagrees.
  1232      The ability to reduce workforce size through a combination of tools 
  1233  does not establish that the current RIF regulations are efficient, 
  1234  clear, or optimal. Workforce reductions may occur through attrition, 
  1235  retirements, voluntary separation incentives, voluntary early 
  1236  retirement authority, term expirations, resignations, or other tools 
  1237  that do not require full part 351 RIF procedures. The question in this 
  1238  rulemaking is not whether agencies can ever reduce headcount under the 
  1239  current framework, but whether the current part 351 RIF process is 
  1240  unnecessarily complex and whether the rules should better enable 
  1241  agencies to retain high performers when a RIF is necessary.
  1242      OPM reasonably concluded that the current RIF framework imposes 
  1243  unnecessary burdens and that the changes in this rule will provide 
  1244  agencies with a more efficient, merit-based process. The revised rules 
  1245  are intended to work alongside other downsizing tools, such as 
  1246  Voluntary Early Retirement Authority (VERA) and Voluntary Separation 
  1247  Incentive Payments (VSIP), and to reduce burden when agencies must 
  1248  invoke RIF procedures.
  1249      Further, as Commenter 0687 noted, voluntary downsizing tools like 
  1250  VERA and VSIP have clear downsides. For example, VERA is only available 
  1251  to those in a narrow eligibility group and can impose burdens on public 
  1252  pension funds. VSIP has a dollar cap that has not been updated since 
  1253  the mid-1990s and which limits its utility as a workforce reshaping 
  1254  tool. With respect to RIFs, as Commenter 0687 noted, the main downside 
  1255  is their complexity and the primacy of non-performance factors like 
  1256  tenure and seniority, meaning that such layoffs are often 
  1257  disproportionately targeted at newer employees that have the most 
  1258  marketable skills. OPM agrees and notes that its revision to the RIF 
  1259  rules addresses these very issues: the complexity of RIFs and the 
  1260  primacy of non-performance factors in determining retention.
  1261      Commenter 0685 observed that one of the more significant 
  1262  consequences of the over-complexity of RIF procedures is that it 
  1263  discourages agencies from utilizing RIF authority even when it may be 
  1264  the most appropriate tool. Commenter 0685 noted that reliance on 
  1265  voluntary separation programs or attrition can be effective in certain 
  1266  contexts, but they do not always provide the level of control or 
  1267  precision needed to align workforce structures with mission 
  1268  requirements. Commenter 0680 argued that the current regulations have 
  1269  been in place for decades and that this longevity shows they work. OPM 
  1270  disagrees. Longevity is not the same as effectiveness. The fact that 
  1271  agencies have struggled for many decades to conduct RIFs under the 
  1272  current rules does not mean the rules are efficient, easy to 
  1273  administer, or properly aligned with modern merit-based workforce 
  1274  needs. OPM reasonably concluded that current rules have not kept pace 
  1275  with the complexity of modern agency missions, organizational 
  1276  structures, funding arrangements, work schedules, hiring authorities, 
  1277  and skill requirements. OPM is not required to keep in place RIF 
  1278  regulations that one longtime former Federal employee described as 
  1279  ``the ultimate bureaucratic poison pill'' merely because they have 
  1280  largely been unchanged for decades. Fred Mills, Civil Disservice: 
  1281  Federal Employment Culture and the Challenge of Genuine Reform, at p. 
  1282  42 (iUniverse 2010).
  1283  
  1284  H. OPM Reasonably Relied on the Department of Defense's Experience as 
  1285  Relevant Support
  1286  
  1287      Commenter 0532 argued that OPM's reliance on Department of Defense 
  1288  (``DOD'') RIF procedures is misplaced because DOD has a separate 
  1289  statutory framework, including congressional-notice provisions for 
  1290  certain RIFs. OPM disagrees.
  1291      DOD is by far the largest employer within the Federal government. 
  1292  It adopted a performance-first RIF system in January 2017. The change 
  1293  was prompted by language in Section 1101 of the National Defense 
  1294  Authorization Act for 2016 directing DOD to make RIF separation 
  1295  decisions ``primarily on the basis of performance.'' The language was 
  1296  codified at 10 U.S.C. 1597(e).
  1297      Congress later revised that language in the FY 2022 NDAA to remove 
  1298  the phrase ``primarily on the basis of performance.'' The current 
  1299  version of 10 U.S.C. 1597(e) instead requires DOD RIF procedures to 
  1300  ``account for employee performance,'' among other factors determined by 
  1301  the Secretary of Defense. But the revision did not prohibit a 
  1302  performance-first system. DOD has retained a performance-first RIF 
  1303  framework, even though its statutory authority currently only requires 
  1304  it to account for employee performance as one factor in RIF retention.
  1305      The existence of this DOD-specific statutory provision does not 
  1306  make DOD's experience irrelevant. OPM remains responsible for 
  1307  prescribing Government-wide RIF regulations under 5 U.S.C. 3502, and it 
  1308  may consider other federal personnel systems in determining whether a 
  1309  revised approach is workable and beneficial.
  1310      Indeed, DOD's current statutory RIF framework no longer requires 
  1311  that it place performance first in determining RIF retention--yet DOD 
  1312  continues to do so, reflecting its judgment that prioritizing 
  1313  performance supports mission readiness and retention of a high-
  1314  performing workforce. DOD's continued use of performance-first after 
  1315  the FY 2022 NDAA undercuts the argument that performance-first RIF 
  1316  retention is legally permissible only when Congress uses the word 
  1317  ``primarily.'' The current DOD statute requires DOD to account for 
  1318  performance among other factors determined by the Secretary, and DOD 
  1319  has continued to implement a performance-first system under that 
  1320  broader language.
  1321      OPM is not importing DOD's statutory scheme wholesale. Rather, 
  1322  DOD's experience serves as powerful evidence that a performance-focused 
  1323  RIF system can support mission readiness and workforce effectiveness. 
  1324  DOD's experience demonstrates that a performance-first RIF system is 
  1325  both administrable and consistent with statutory direction to consider 
  1326  multiple retention factors. OPM reasonably relies on that experience in 
  1327  elevating performance in governmentwide RIF retention standing while 
  1328  continuing to give effect to tenure, veterans' preference, and length 
  1329  of service.
  1330      Further, OPM believes there is an independent interest in ensuring 
  1331  some level of consistency across government in RIF procedures, in that 
  1332  all agencies should place performance first in determining RIF 
  1333  retention.
  1334  
  1335  I. This Final Rule Does Not Violate the APA Because the Proposed Rule 
  1336  Was Issued Alongside Other Rulemakings
  1337  
  1338      Several commenters argued that OPM's RIF procedures proposal should 
  1339  have been issued in a single consolidated rulemaking with OPM's 
  1340  separate proposals concerning performance appraisal and RIF appeals. 
  1341  Commenter 0532, for example, argued that OPM's RIF proposal must be 
  1342  viewed together with OPM's separate proposals concerning RIF appeals 
  1343  and performance appraisal, and that OPM violated the APA by issuing the
  1344  
  1345  [[Page 49189]]
  1346  
  1347  proposals separately. OPM has considered these comments and disagrees 
  1348  that the Administrative Procedure Act (``APA'') required OPM to combine 
  1349  the rulemakings, delay this rulemaking, reopen the comment period, or 
  1350  provide a separate comment period devoted solely to the interaction 
  1351  among the three proposals.
  1352      The APA requires a notice of proposed rulemaking to identify the 
  1353  time, place, and nature of the proceeding, the legal authority for the 
  1354  proposal, and either the proposed rule's terms or substance or a 
  1355  description of the subjects and issues involved; after notice, the 
  1356  agency must provide interested persons an opportunity to submit written 
  1357  data, views, or arguments and must consider relevant matter presented. 
  1358  5 U.S.C. 553(b)-(c). The RIF proposal satisfied those requirements. It 
  1359  identified the statutory authorities for the rulemaking, identified the 
  1360  affected CFR Parts, described the proposed changes to the RIF 
  1361  regulations and related provisions, provided proposed regulatory text, 
  1362  invited public comment on the RIF proposal, and set a comment deadline. 
  1363  In addition, OPM provided a section in the proposed rule titled ``Other 
  1364  regulatory changes'' that identified the concurrent rulemakings with 
  1365  respect to RIF appeals and performance appraisals as potentially 
  1366  intersecting with the current rulemakings.
  1367      The APA does not require an agency to combine every related 
  1368  regulatory initiative into a single notice-and-comment proceeding. 
  1369  Agencies routinely address related but distinct issues in separate 
  1370  rulemakings, particularly where the rules amend different regulatory 
  1371  provisions, address different legal questions, rest on different 
  1372  administrative records, and can operate independently. That is the case 
  1373  here. This rule concerns the substantive procedures for conducting 
  1374  RIFs, including RIF coverage, retention standing, release from 
  1375  competitive level, assignment rights, notices, RPL, CTAP, ICTAP, 
  1376  transfers of function, and related conforming provisions. The 
  1377  performance-appraisal proposal concerned the standards and procedures 
  1378  for rating employee performance under part 430. The RIF appeals 
  1379  proposal concerned the forum and procedures for administrative review 
  1380  of RIF actions. Those subjects are related, but they are not the same 
  1381  rulemaking.
  1382      The fact that OPM also proposed related personnel-management 
  1383  reforms around the same time does not make the RIF proposal 
  1384  procedurally defective. Agencies may address related subjects in 
  1385  separate rulemakings, particularly where, as here, the rulemakings 
  1386  address distinct regulatory parts and distinct issues: RIF retention

  1388  Indeed, OPM's proposals involving performance appraisal and RIF appeals 
  1389  have separate administrative records, involve separate regulatory 
  1390  provisions, tackle distinct issues and problems, and are based on 
  1391  distinct justifications.
  1392      Nor did OPM conceal the existence or potential relevance of the

[2026-15665: lines 1544-1943 of 6220, FR page 49190]
  1544  A. Part 351, Subpart B: Changes in Definitions, Coverage, Use of 
  1545  Regulations, and Agency Responsibilities
  1546  
  1547  1. Erosion of Duties Reclassifications
  1548      OPM is modifying Sec.  351.201(a)(2) to remove from the list of 
  1549  actions that require agencies to use RIF procedures reclassification of 
  1550  an employee's position due to erosion of duties if the action would 
  1551  take effect after an agency had formally announced a RIF in the 
  1552  employee's competitive area and the RIF would take effect within 180 
  1553  days.
  1554      Commenter 0532 argued that OPM has not justified removing erosion-
  1555  of-duties reclassifications from the actions requiring RIF procedures. 
  1556  OPM disagrees.
  1557      The proposed rule explains the history of the erosion-of-duties 
  1558  provision. In 1986, OPM generally removed erosion-of-duties 
  1559  reclassifications from the categories of actions subject to RIF 
  1560  procedures, but retained a narrow RIF-procedure requirement for 
  1561  reclassifications occurring after announcement of a RIF and within 180 
  1562  days of the RIF effective date. OPM is now removing that narrow 
  1563  procedural trigger because it is unreasonable and impracticable to 
  1564  require agencies to build a retention register for such 
  1565  reclassifications, and OPM is not aware of any agency actually 
  1566  executing an erosion-of-duties reclassification action using RIF 
  1567  procedures since the 1986 revision.
  1568      Commenter 0037 argued that the ``erosion of duties'' changes could 
  1569  be used to constructively demote disfavored employees. OPM disagrees. 
  1570  Erosion of duties reclassifications have generally been excluded from 
  1571  RIF procedures since 1986, except in the narrow circumstance where the 
  1572  reclassification will take effect after an agency has formally 
  1573  announced a RIF in the employee's competitive area that will take 
  1574  effect within 180 days. This rule directly addresses concerns that 
  1575  erosion-of-duties reclassifications could be used to undermine the RIF 
  1576  retention order. Rather than requiring a full RIF process for erosion-
  1577  of-duties reclassifications, this rule will bar agencies from 
  1578  undertaking an erosion-of-duties reclassification between the formal 
  1579  announcement and completion of a RIF if the action would adversely 
  1580  affect an employee's retention standing in the RIF. This is a more 
  1581  direct and administrable safeguard than the current rule. Notably, 
  1582  commenters 0037 and 0532 do not identify any concrete instance in which 
  1583  the existing erosion-of-duties RIF trigger has been necessary to 
  1584  protect employees, nor do
  1585  
  1586  [[Page 49191]]
  1587  
  1588  commenters 0037 or 0532 explain why the proposed anti-manipulation 
  1589  prohibition would be inadequate.
  1590      Instead, OPM agrees with Commenter 0720, a Federal agency, that the 
  1591  current erosion-of-duties provision is outdated, and OPM's approach in 
  1592  this rule ``reduces unnecessary confusion and risk while preserving 
  1593  safeguards against improper alterations to retention outcomes.''
  1594  2. Employees Excluded From RIF Competition
  1595      This rule modifies the definition of the term Competing employee in 
  1596  Sec.  351.203 to mean an employee in the competitive service tenure 
  1597  group or the excepted service tenure group. It also adds a definition 
  1598  of Competitive service tenure group to mean all employees within 
  1599  competitive service tenure subgroups I and II; that is, all employees 
  1600  in the competitive service who, as of the date of the RIF notice, are 
  1601  not serving an initial probationary period or a temporary appointment 
  1602  of 1 year or less under subpart D of 5 CFR part 316. This rule defines 
  1603  the Excepted service tenure group as all employees within excepted 
  1604  service tenure subgroups I and II; that is, all excepted service 
  1605  appointees serving in a career position (that is, not in Schedule C or 
  1606  G) who, as of the date of the RIF notice, are not serving a trial 
  1607  period or in a temporary or time-limited appointment of 1 year or less.
  1608      OPM is also adding definitions of initial probationary period and 
  1609  trial period to Sec.  351.203. With respect to these provisions, OPM 
  1610  notes that a supervisory or managerial employee with career tenure who 
  1611  is only on probation with respect to those supervisory or managerial 
  1612  functions (i.e., is entitled to be returned to a nonsupervisory or non-
  1613  managerial position rather than being subject to removal under 5 CFR 
  1614  part 315, subpart I) would be included in the RIF in the supervisory or 
  1615  managerial position, and would not be subject to the exclusion from RIF 
  1616  procedures applicable to individuals serving an initial probationary 
  1617  period under 5 CFR 11.2. Further, an employee who is serving both an 
  1618  initial probationary period and a supervisory probationary period 
  1619  simultaneously is exempt from RIF procedures.
  1620      In the proposed rule, OPM proposed to add a Sec.  351.202(d) that 
  1621  lists categories of employees excluded from RIF retention procedures, 
  1622  as they fall outside the definition of ``competing employees'' under 5 
  1623  U.S.C. 3502(a). Under OPM's definition of ``competing employees,'' 
  1624  employees in the competitive service who are serving an initial 
  1625  probationary period would be excluded from RIF procedures, as would 
  1626  employees in the excepted service who are serving a trial period. In 
  1627  addition, competitive and excepted service employees who are serving 
  1628  temporary or time-limited appointments of 1 year or less would be 
  1629  excluded from RIF competition, as would Schedule C and Schedule G 
  1630  employees.
  1631      In this final rule, OPM is revising the wording of Sec.  
  1632  351.202(d). The revised wording narrows Sec.  351.202(d) from a broad 
  1633  statement that certain employees are excluded from part 351 altogether 
  1634  to a more precise statement that they are not ``competing employees'' 
  1635  for RIF purposes. The final rule clarifies the consequences of this 
  1636  classification: an agency may retain such an employee while releasing a 
  1637  competing employee, and may furlough, separate, demote, or reassign 
  1638  such an employee for a reason described in Sec.  351.201(a)(2) (lack of 
  1639  work, shortage of funds, insufficient personnel ceiling, 
  1640  reorganization, or the exercise of reemployment rights or restoration 
  1641  rights) without determining the employee's retention standing under 
  1642  subparts D and E, applying the order-of-release provisions in subpart 
  1643  F, or providing assignment rights under subpart G, provided the action 
  1644  is otherwise consistent with the terms of the employee's appointment 
  1645  and applicable law. Further, the revised text clarifies that these 
  1646  excluded employees are still subject to the notice provisions of Sec.  
  1647  351.801 where they are furloughed for more than 30 days, separated, 
  1648  demoted, or reassigned for the reasons described in Sec.  
  1649  351.201(a)(2), and the action is not merely the expiration of a 
  1650  temporary or time-limited appointment according to its terms. Under 
  1651  such circumstances the agency must provide the employee a modified 
  1652  written notice that includes the action to be taken, the reasons for 
  1653  the action, and its effective date; a link to 5 CFR part 351 and access 
  1654  to the agency's records pertinent to the reduction in force being 
  1655  taken; information on reemployment rights; and any appeal rights.
  1656      In addition, the final rule makes other wording changes to Sec.  
  1657  351.202(d). It revises the Schedule C and Schedule G language by 
  1658  referring to employees ``serving under'' those appointments and removes 
  1659  a proposed reference to term appointments under part 316 subpart C, 
  1660  making clear that the competitive-service temporary-appointment 
  1661  exclusion is limited to temporary appointments of 1 year or less under 
  1662  part 316 subpart D.
  1663      Commenter 0719, a Federal agency, supported the proposed changes 
  1664  excluding initial probationary period and trial period employees from 
  1665  RIF competition, noting that the current RIF rules demand that 
  1666  probationary and trial period employees be released first in a RIF. 
  1667  Commenter 0719 noted that this results in ``the loss of high potential 
  1668  individuals essential for long term succession planning and mission 
  1669  continuity.'' The agency noted that ``[r]emoving these groups from RIF 
  1670  competition will allow [it] greater flexibility to retain high 
  1671  potential early career employees even in constrained budget 
  1672  conditions.'' Commenter 0687 noted that termination of probationary 
  1673  employees as part of workforce reshaping activities can ``weaken[] 
  1674  early career pipelines'' and result in the loss of some of the agency's 
  1675  ``best talent.'' OPM agrees.
  1676      Commenter 0678 claimed that these exclusions would mean that the 
  1677  RIF regulations would no longer provide a comprehensive system to 
  1678  govern workforce reductions, while Commenter 0684 argued that this 
  1679  change would conflict with 5 U.S.C. 3501(b)'s broad coverage provision. 
  1680  OPM disagrees. OPM has long used its authority under 5 U.S.C. 3502 to 
  1681  define the otherwise-undefined statutory term ``competing employees'' 
  1682  subject to RIF competition to exclude certain groups of employees from 
  1683  RIF retention procedures. For example, in its regulations at 5 CFR 
  1684  316.911, OPM recognizes that employees ``whose initial appointment [is] 
  1685  for a period of 1 year or less are not assigned a tenure group and do 
  1686  not compete with other employees in a RIF.'' In its regulations at 5 
  1687  CFR 353.209, OPM stated that an employee performing duty with the 
  1688  uniformed services ``is not a `competing employee' under'' the RIF 
  1689  regulations. And OPM's regulations at 5 CFR 351.705 have long provided 
  1690  that an agency may, but is not required to, provide assignment rights 
  1691  to excepted service employees.
  1692      Related statutory provisions, and the broader history of 
  1693  probationary and trial periods in the Federal service, support OPM's 
  1694  determination that probationary and trial period employees should not 
  1695  be considered ``competing employees'' for purposes of 5 U.S.C. 3502. 
  1696  The phrase ``competing employee'' in 5 U.S.C. 3502 must be read against 
  1697  a long background tracing to the Pendleton Act of 1883 whereby Congress 
  1698  has consistently and deliberately maintained a distinction between 
  1699  employees whose appointments have become final and employees still 
  1700  serving a probationary or trial period. This distinction reflects a 
  1701  longstanding congressional and regulatory judgment that competitive 
  1702  selection alone is not the final test of fitness for Federal
  1703  
  1704  [[Page 49192]]
  1705  
  1706  service. Rather, an initial period of actual service has always served 
  1707  as the Government's final opportunity to determine whether an employee 
  1708  should receive the full procedural protections associated with 
  1709  continuing Federal employment.
  1710      The Pendleton Act (22 Stat. 403) required that the ``there shall be 
  1711  a period of probation before any absolute appointment or employment 
  1712  aforesaid.'' That statutory formulation indicates that Congress did not 
  1713  treat appointment and final appointment as the same event. It preserved 
  1714  a two-step process--competitive appointment first, with final 
  1715  appointment only after satisfactory completion of probation.
  1716      In its first annual report in 1884, the Civil Service Commission 
  1717  characterized the probationary period as lasting ``six months before 
  1718  any absolute appointment can be made. At the end of this time the 
  1719  appointee goes out of the service unless then reappointed.'' \7\ Two 
  1720  years later, the Commission wrote in its third annual report that 
  1721  ``doing the public work is precisely what the Merit System provides. If 
  1722  at its termination the appointing officer is not . . . willing to make 
  1723  an unconditional appointment, the probationer is . . . absolutely out 
  1724  of the service without any action on the part of the Government.'' \8\
  1725  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  1726  
  1727      \7\ First Annual Report of the United States Civil Service 
  1728  Commission to the President (1884), p. 29, https://babel.hathitrust.org/cgi/pt?id=nnc1.cu09006737&seq=9.
  1729      \8\ Third Annual Report of the United States Civil Service 
  1730  Commission to the President (1886), p. 36, https://babel.hathitrust.org/cgi/pt?id=njp.32101073361022&seq=40.
  1731  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  1732  
  1733      With the enactment of the Lloyd-La Follette Act of 1912, Congress 
  1734  created the first legislative codification of protection against 
  1735  removal for civil servants. The Act established ``[t]hat no person in 
  1736  the classified civil service of the United States shall be removed 
  1737  therefrom except for such cause as will promote the efficiency of said 
  1738  service.'' \9\ The Act also imposed certain procedural requirements on 
  1739  removals including advance notice and an opportunity to respond in 
  1740  writing. However, Congress did not establish employment protections for 
  1741  probationary employees, and has maintained this exclusion through every 
  1742  subsequent recodification of the civil service laws.
  1743  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  1744  
  1745      \9\ The Lloyd-La Follette Act, 37 Stat. 555 (1912), as amended, 
  1746  62 Stat. 354 (1948), 5 U.S.C.A. 652(a).
  1747  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  1748  
  1749      Congress legislated against this backdrop in using the term 
  1750  ``competing employees'' in the Veterans' Preference Act of 1944 \10\--
  1751  the direct legislative predecessor of 5 U.S.C. 3502. The Veterans' 
  1752  Preference Act of 1944 did not define ``competing employees'' to 
  1753  include all individuals serving in Federal positions. Instead, Section 
  1754  12 of that Act provided that, in a reduction in personnel, ``competing 
  1755  employees'' would be released in accordance with Civil Service 
  1756  Commission regulations giving due effect to the statutory retention 
  1757  factors. Congress thus left the identification of the competitive group 
  1758  to regulation.
  1759  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  1760  
  1761      \10\ Public Law 78-359, 58 Stat. 387 (codified, as amended in 
  1762  part, at 5 U.S.C. 3309-3320).
  1763  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  1764  
  1765      This is particularly significant because, in Section 14, the 
  1766  Veterans' Preference Act expanded civil service protections to 
  1767  preference eligible Federal employees, but it explicitly excluded 
  1768  probationers, limiting its protections to a ``permanent or indefinite 
  1769  preference eligible, who has completed a probationary or trial 
  1770  period.'' Section 12 and section 14 were enacted in the same statute. 
  1771  If Congress believed probationary and trial-period employees 
  1772  necessarily had to be treated the same as final appointees for all 
  1773  retention-related purposes, it would be odd for Congress, two sections 
  1774  later, to condition major procedural protections on completion of 
  1775  probationary or trial service. The better reading is that the 1944 Act 
  1776  preserved a two-step civil-service model: an employee could enter 
  1777  Federal service and receive whatever preference rights the statute and 
  1778  regulations afforded, but the employee did not necessarily become part 
  1779  of the competitive retention workforce before completing the 
  1780  probationary or trial period.
  1781      The statutory text of 5 U.S.C. 3502(a) therefore does not compel 
  1782  OPM to include employees serving an initial probationary or trial 
  1783  period in RIF competition; rather, it permits OPM to determine by 
  1784  regulation that such employees are not ``competing employees'' for 
  1785  purposes of retention registers and order of release, while preserving 
  1786  any independently applicable statutory or regulatory protections.\11\
  1787  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  1788  
  1789      \11\ Commenter 0684 points to Fathauer v. United States, 566 
  1790  F.3d 1352 (Fed. Cir. 2009), but that case is inapposite. Here, OPM 
  1791  is not defining ``employee'' in 5 U.S.C. 3501(b) to nullify 
  1792  statutory coverage. Instead, it is defining the narrower, undefined 
  1793  term ``competing employee'' in section 3502(a), a term Congress 
  1794  expressly left for implementation through OPM regulations.
  1795  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  1796  
  1797      The current 5 U.S.C. 7511 codifies the longstanding exclusion of 
  1798  probationary and trial period employees from the adverse-action 
  1799  definition of ``employee.'' Under 5 U.S.C. 7511, an ``employee'' in the 
  1800  competitive service or excepted service generally means an individual 
  1801  who is not serving a probationary or trial period under an initial 
  1802  appointment or who has completed one year of current continuous service 
  1803  under other than a temporary appointment limited to one year or less.
  1804      Courts interpreting section 7511 and related CSRA provisions have 
  1805  repeatedly recognized that Congress intended agencies to retain 
  1806  substantial flexibility over probationary and trial-period employees. 
  1807  In Department of Justice v. FLRA, the D.C. Circuit relied on the CSRA's 
  1808  structure and legislative history in concluding that probationary 
  1809  employees could not obtain through negotiated grievance procedures the 
  1810  kind of review Congress deliberately withheld from them in chapter 
  1811  75.\12\ 709 F.2d 724, 730 (D.C. Cir. 1983). In United States v. 
  1812  Connolly, the Federal Circuit likewise treated the exclusion of 
  1813  probationary employees from chapter 75 appeal rights as a deliberate 
  1814  congressional choice, not a statutory gap for courts or agencies to 
  1815  fill.\13\ And in National Treasury Employees Union v. FLRA, the D.C. 
  1816  Circuit reaffirmed that the CSRA's treatment of probationary employees 
  1817  reflects Congress's judgment that agencies must have latitude to assess 
  1818  and separate employees who have not yet completed the testing period 
  1819  for Federal service.\14\ This history does not mean that section 7511 
  1820  directly controls chapter 35 RIF procedures. It does, however, confirm 
  1821  that OPM's treatment of probationary, trial-period, and short-term 
  1822  temporary employees in this rule is consistent with the broader civil-
  1823  service framework Congress enacted.
  1824  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  1825  
  1826      \12\ See Dep't of Justice v. FLRA, 709 F.2d 724, 730 (D.C. Cir. 
  1827  1983).
  1828      \13\ See U.S. v. Connolly, 716 F.2d 882, 886 (Fed. Cir. 1983).
  1829      \14\ See Nat'l Treasury Emps. Union v. FLRA, 848 F.2d 1273, 1275 
  1830  (D.C. Cir. 1988).
  1831  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  1832  
  1833      In addition, 5 U.S.C. 3502 should be read consistent with 5 U.S.C. 
  1834  3321, which contemplates a probationary period before an appointment 
  1835  becomes final and allows the President to issue rules and regulations 
  1836  effectuating probationary periods. Current Civil Service Rule 11, 
  1837  issued by the President under Executive Order (E.O.) 14284, already 
  1838  supplies a comprehensive framework for probationary and trial-period 
  1839  employment. It requires agencies to use probationary and trial periods 
  1840  to evaluate whether an employee's continuation in Federal service 
  1841  advances the public interest and expressly permits agencies to consider 
  1842  agency needs and interests, whether continued employment would advance 
  1843  agency or Government organizational goals, and whether continued
  1844  
  1845  [[Page 49193]]
  1846  
  1847  employment would advance the efficiency of the service.
  1848      Those considerations substantially overlap with the reasons 
  1849  agencies conduct RIFs, including lack of work, shortage of funds, and 
  1850  reorganization. Requiring agencies to apply full part 351 retention-
  1851  register, order-of-release, and assignment-right procedures to 
  1852  employees whose appointments have not yet become final would duplicate 
  1853  Rule 11 and could produce inconsistent outcomes. For example, Rule 11 
  1854  might support retaining a probationary employee because the employee 
  1855  has scarce skills, strong actual performance, and is needed for the 
  1856  agency's future mission. But a part 351 retention register would likely 
  1857  place the same employee low because the employee has little service 
  1858  time and may lack a rating of record. Thus, excluding probationary and 
  1859  trial period employees from the statutory definition of ``competing 
  1860  employees'' in 5 U.S.C. 3502(a) eliminates duplication and makes sense 
  1861  of the overall statutory scheme.
  1862      With respect to temporary employees, OPM's regulations at 5 CFR 
  1863  part 316, subpart D make clear that such appointments are only 
  1864  appropriate to meet short-term needs, including ``for such reasons as 
  1865  abolishment, reorganization, or contracting of the function, 
  1866  anticipated reduction in funding, or completion of a specific project 
  1867  or peak workload.'' 5 CFR 316.401(a)(2). Further, ``[t]he supervisor of 
  1868  each position filled by temporary appointment must certify that the 
  1869  employment need is truly temporary and that the proposed appointment 
  1870  meets the regulatory time limits.'' Id. 316.401(b). Thus, these 
  1871  regulations indicate that temporary employees do not have a reasonable 
  1872  expectation of long-term employment and thus should not be considered 
  1873  ``competing employees'' for purposes of 5 U.S.C. 3502.
  1874      Further, in the final rule, OPM has clarified that the employees 
  1875  excluded from RIF competition are not entirely outside the regulatory 
  1876  scheme and must receive a notice in accordance with 5 U.S.C. 3502(d) 
  1877  when they are furloughed for more than 30 days, separated, demoted, or 
  1878  reassigned for reasons of lack of work, shortage of funds, insufficient 
  1879  personnel ceiling, reorganization, or the exercise of reemployment 
  1880  rights or restoration rights and the action is not merely the 
  1881  expiration of a temporary or time-limited appointment according to its 
  1882  terms. In addition, the regulations provide in Sec.  351.605 that all 
  1883  positions in the competitive area, including those of employees 
  1884  excluded from RIF competition under Sec.  351.202(d), must be abolished 
  1885  within 180 days for an agency to permissibly use the streamlined 
  1886  procedures of that subpart.
  1887      Commenter 0672 objected that probationary employees can be covered 
  1888  by the proposal's missing-rating rules and therefore should remain in 
  1889  RIF competition. OPM does not agree that the proposed modal-rating 
  1890  provision eliminates the need to exclude probationary and trial-period 
  1891  employees from RIF competition. The modal-rating rule is a limited 
  1892  proxy for competing employees who lack ratings in the applicable 
  1893  lookback period; it does not provide an individualized measure of 
  1894  performance for employees whose appointments have not yet been 
  1895  finalized and who often have not served long enough to receive a rating 
  1896  of record. In a performance-first RIF system, assigning retention 
  1897  standing to such employees based on the most common rating assigned to 
  1898  other employees would fail to measure the employee's own performance. 
  1899  OPM therefore reasonably treats probationary and trial-period employees 
  1900  outside the retention-register process and permits agencies to retain, 
  1901  finalize, or separate them under the rules applicable to their 
  1902  appointments, instead of the RIF rules.
  1903      Further, the modal-rating approach does not address the separate 
  1904  legal and personnel-management function of probationary and trial 
  1905  periods. Civil Service Rule 11 provides that agencies must use 
  1906  probationary and trial periods to evaluate an employee's fitness and 
  1907  whether continued employment advances the public interest; the agency 
  1908  may consider performance and conduct, agency needs, organizational 
  1909  goals, and efficiency of the service before finalizing the appointment. 
  1910  A modal RIF rating cannot replace that appointment-finalization 
  1911  judgment. It does not tell the agency whether the employee has 
  1912  demonstrated sufficient fitness, adaptability, conduct, judgment, or 
  1913  mission fit to warrant final appointment. It simply imputes a rating 
  1914  based on how other employees were rated. That is a poor fit for 
  1915  employees who are still in the government's final assessment period.
  1916      Commenters 0674 and 0680 argued that excluding temporary, 
  1917  probationary and trial period employees from RIF procedures could mean 
  1918  that certain employees still covered by RIF regulations would be 
  1919  released ahead of more junior employees, thus undermining tenure as a 
  1920  statutory retention factor. But 5 U.S.C. 3502 does not prescribe a 
  1921  strict ``last in, first out'' system. It does not define ``competing 
  1922  employees,'' does not require every employee in an agency to compete 
  1923  against every other employee, and does not require agencies to retain 
  1924  every more senior employee ahead of every less senior employee in all 
  1925  circumstances. Instead, it directed OPM to create regulations for the 
  1926  release of competing employees and to give ``due effect'' to several 
  1927  factors. ``Due effect'' does not mean controlling effect, equal effect,

  2013  4. Transfers of Function
  2014      OPM is revising Sec.  351.203 to modify the definition of transfer 
  2015  of function to adhere to the text of the applicable statute enacted by 
  2016  Congress to govern transfers of function, 5 U.S.C. 3503. That statute 
  2017  only applies to a situation ``[w]hen a function is transferred from one 
  2018  agency to another . . . .'' (emphasis added).
  2019      Commenters 0672 and 0674 argued that narrowing transfer-of-function 
  2020  procedures would weaken employee protections and allow agencies to 
  2021  evade RIF rules through internal reorganizations. OPM disagrees. This 
  2022  rule does not allow agencies to evade RIF requirements when an internal 
  2023  reorganization results in release from a competitive level for RIF 
  2024  reasons. Rather, it distinguishes between interagency transfers of 
  2025  function, where governmentwide transfer-of-function protections are 
  2026  statutorily required, and internal management realignments, where 
  2027  ordinary reassignment principles can address any resulting personnel 
  2028  actions and offer adequate protections for employees. Specifically, 
  2029  transfers and reassignments of employees in the competitive service 
  2030  within agencies will continue to be governed by 5 CFR part 335. 
  2031  Transfers and reassignments of employees within agencies in the 
  2032  excepted service will continue to be governed by 5 CFR parts 213 and 
  2033  302. Further, 5 U.S.C. 2301 requires agencies to adhere to Merit System 
  2034  Principles in personnel management, including transfers and 
  2035  reassignments of employees, and in the final rule OPM is amending Sec.  
  2036  351.204 to provide specifically that its 5 CFR part 351 regulations 
  2037  must be administered and applied consistent with all applicable laws, 
  2038  including the Merit System Principles set forth in 5 U.S.C. 2301(b).
  2039      Commenter 0719, a Federal agency, stated that ``[t]he updated 
  2040  definition for transfer of function will remove constraints that 
  2041  currently impede timely organizational adjustments,'' noting that 
  2042  existing rules result in ``administrative obstacles that slow [its] 
  2043  ability to adapt quickly to emerging needs.'' Commenter 0719 noted 
  2044  that, ``[u]nder existing regulations, even straightforward internal 
  2045  realignments can require extensive procedures, discouraging agencies 
  2046  from implementing changes that could reduce duplication, improve 
  2047  efficiency, or better align staff with mission priorities.'' OPM 
  2048  agrees.
  2049  5. Other Definitions
  2050      In this rule, OPM is providing a formal definition of ``reduction 
  2051  in force'': the release of a competing employee from his or her 
  2052  competitive level by furlough for more than 30 days, separation, or 
  2053  demotion, or reassignment requiring displacement, when the release is 
  2054  required because of lack of work; shortage of funds; insufficient 
  2055  personnel ceiling; reorganization; or the exercise of reemployment 
  2056  rights or restoration rights. OPM did not receive significant comments 
  2057  regarding its definition of ``reduction in force,'' as this definition 
  2058  closely tracks the longstanding coverage of OPM's RIF regulations, as 
  2059  reflected in 5 CFR 351.201(a)(2).
  2060      This rule modifies the current definitions in Sec.  351.203 for 
  2061  current rating of record and rating of record. The revision to current 
  2062  rating of record updates the cross reference within part 351. The

  2064  evaluation--and not a mid-year within-grade evaluation--can be used 
  2065  when computing the performance credit, which is used for determining 
  2066  standing on the retention register. OPM did not receive significant

  2068      OPM is also adding meanings for agency, Government obligation and 
  2069  military spouse, and to correct a typo in Sec.  351.204 to change 
  2070  ``reduction force'' to ``reduction in force.'' OPM did not receive 
  2071  significant adverse comment regarding these proposed changes. As

  2073  restoration protected employee.

  2075  provision to state clearly that agencies may not manipulate competitive

  2089  B. Part 351, Subpart C: Changes in Transfer of Function Procedures
  2090  
  2091      OPM is substituting the word ``agency'' for ``competitive area''

  2093  align with the text of the statute Congress enacted governing transfers

  2095  between agencies, not within agencies. Notably, the regulations 
  2096  governing transfers of function applicable to the SES apply only to

  2137  C. Part 351, Subpart D: Changes in How Competitive Areas Are Defined 
  2138  and Approved
  2139  
  2140      This rule revises Sec.  351.402(b) to allow agencies to designate a 
  2141  competitive area as being any organizational unit, or combination of 
  2142  organizational units, on an agency's official organizational chart. 
  2143  Organizational charts must be available on the agency's public facing 
  2144  web page or otherwise appropriately documented by the agency. An 
  2145  organizational unit for these purposes must be designated/approved by 
  2146  the head of the agency, or designee, and the designation or approval 
  2147  cannot be redelegated to an official below the agency's headquarters 
  2148  level.
  2149      In addition, OPM is revising Sec.  351.402(b) to require that an 
  2150  organizational unit for purposes of a RIF must be clearly distinguished 
  2151  from other organizational units with regard to its operation, work 
  2152  function, staff, and supervisory oversight. In addition, OPM is 
  2153  clarifying that field or regional offices officially established by the 
  2154  agency as discrete organizational units and shown on the agency's 
  2155  official organizational chart may be their own competitive area(s).
  2156      Commenter 0684 contended that the previous regulatory phrase 
  2157  ``under separate administration'' was not vague but had an accepted 
  2158  meaning as encompassing ``the authority to take or direct personnel 
  2159  actions.'' Commenter 0684 argued that the requirement in this rule that 
  2160  an organizational unit be differentiated from other organizational 
  2161  units with regard to its operation, work function, staff, and 
  2162  supervisory oversight is not equivalent to the previous phrase.
  2163      However, the previous OPM rulemaking and Federal Circuit case cited 
  2164  by Commenter 0684 state that ``under separate administration'' may be 
  2165  satisfied by as little as the authority to ``assign duties,'' a power 
  2166  that any front-line supervisor would possess. Further, OPM's current 
  2167  Workforce Reshaping Operations Handbook rejects Commenter 0684's 
  2168  definition of ``under separate administration,'' as OPM states that the 
  2169  definition ``[r]ecognizes that individual organizational components may 
  2170  be under separate administration even though many agencies reserve 
  2171  final approval of certain personnel actions to a higher level in the 
  2172  agency.'' \15\ Ultimately, Commenter 0684 only underscores that the 
  2173  phrase ``under separate administration'' is confusing, and that OPM was 
  2174  correct in the proposed rule in stating that ``the current terminology 
  2175  is not aligned with the operational realities of Federal agencies, 
  2176  where many components may be `under separate administration' in some 
  2177  important respects, but under centralized administration in other 
  2178  important respects.''
  2179  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  2180  
  2181      \15\ OPM, Workforce Reshaping Operations Handbook, at pp. 30-31, 
  2182  https://www.opm.gov/policy-data-oversight/workforce-restructuring/reductions-in-force-rif/workforce_reshaping.pdf.

  2184  
  2185      Commenter 0684 also contended that Sec.  351.402(b) ``no longer 
  2186  specifies that the definition is the minimum competitive area, and thus 
  2187  strips agencies of the flexibility to expand a small competitive area 
  2188  to allow for competition.'' But that is not so: section 351.402(b) 
  2189  continues to state that a ``competitive area may consist of any 
  2190  organizational unit or combination of units established on the agency's 
  2191  official organizational chart,'' which allows agencies to expand a 
  2192  small competitive area to allow for greater competition.
  2193      Commenter 0687 expressed appreciation that ``OPM is taking 
  2194  competitive area manipulation seriously and agree[d] with OPM's stated 
  2195  intent to preserve rules against it,'' but presented several issues 
  2196  with OPM's new proposed definition. The commenter noted that Federal 
  2197  agencies are not required to maintain a single ``official'' 
  2198  organizational chart, and in practice agencies or their subparts may 
  2199  maintain several organizational charts for different purposes, which 
  2200  may not reflect how the agency manages itself on a day-to-day basis. 
  2201  Therefore, Commenter 0687 suggested that OPM
  2202  
  2203  [[Page 49196]]
  2204  
  2205  ``pick a single, authoritative dataset for the purposes of competitive 
  2206  area definition: the hierarchy utilized during administration of the 
  2207  Federal Employee Viewpoint Survey [FEVS] in the most immediately prior 
  2208  year.''
  2209      OPM appreciates Commenter 0687's suggestion but does not adopt it. 
  2210  OPM believes that administration of FEVS should remain flexible and 
  2211  responsive to agency needs and not be tied to administration of RIFs. 
  2212  OPM also believes that agencies may reasonably adopt new organizational 
  2213  charts that deviate from the structure reflected in their previous 
  2214  year's administration of FEVS based on evolving mission needs, 
  2215  including changes in agency budgets, technology, and presidential and 
  2216  congressional priorities. Indeed, the RIF regulations have long applied 
  2217  where release is required due to, inter alia, ``reorganization,'' see 5 
  2218  CFR 351.201(a)(2), defined as ``the planned elimination, addition, or 
  2219  redistribution of functions or duties in an organization,'' see 5 CFR 
  2220  351.203. OPM believes that the limitations in Sec.  351.402(c) against 
  2221  recognizing new competitive areas that will be in effect for less than 
  2222  90 days before issuance of RIF notices, as augmented by changes 
  2223  described below, provide sufficient guardrails against competitive area 
  2224  manipulation.
  2225      Commenter 0683 also expressed concern about the ``potential for 
  2226  gerrymandering competitive areas to target particular employees or 
  2227  groups of employees.'' It suggested that ``OPM require agencies to 
  2228  establish competitive area designations through a transparent process, 
  2229  with documentation available for review, and to prohibit agencies from 
  2230  establishing or modifying competitive areas after a decision to conduct 
  2231  a RIF has been made.''
  2232      OPM agrees with this suggestion, in part. In this final rule, OPM 
  2233  is adding an additional safeguard against competitive area 
  2234  manipulation: when agencies are seeking approval from OPM for a new 
  2235  competitive area that has existed for less than 90 days prior to 
  2236  issuing specific RIF notices, the agency shall submit a description of 
  2237  the competitive area, along with a written statement explaining the 
  2238  bona fide organizational basis for the competitive area, to OPM for 
  2239  approval in advance of the RIF. Such approval is also required where an 
  2240  agency materially modifies a competitive area. In addition, 
  2241  descriptions of all competitive areas, and accompanying explanations 
  2242  submitted to OPM, must be made readily available for review consistent 
  2243  with national security considerations and applicable laws including the 
  2244  Freedom of Information Act (5 U.S.C. 552), and the Privacy Act (5 
  2245  U.S.C. 552a). In addition, as noted above, OPM is requiring expressly 
  2246  that the RIF regulations be administered consistent with the merit 
  2247  system principles set forth in 5 U.S.C. 2301. OPM believes that these 
  2248  suggestions adequately address the concerns expressed by Commenters 
  2249  0683 and 0687 regarding competitive area manipulation. These further 
  2250  advance Commenter 0685's call for OPM to ``strengthen requirements 
  2251  related to transparency and documentation'' in the final rule.
  2252  
  2253  D. Part 351, Subpart E: New Method of Deriving Retention Standing, 
  2254  Revised Order of Retention Examples, and Additional Examples
  2255  
  2256      OPM is finalizing its changes to 5 CFR part 351, subpart E 
  2257  ``Retention Standing,'' including revised and reorganized content in 
  2258  Sec. Sec.  351.501 through 351.504. In addition, OPM is renumbering 
  2259  current Sec.  351.505 Records and Sec.  351.506 Effective date of 
  2260  retention standing to Sec.  351.506 Records and Sec.  351.507 Effective 
  2261  date of retention standing, respectively.
  2262      As noted above, under this rule (and particularly Sec.  351.501 
  2263  Order of retention), when determining the order in which employees are 
  2264  placed on a RIF retention register, agencies will now do so based on 
  2265  whether the employee is in the competitive service tenure group or 
  2266  excepted service tenure group. Within each group, employees will be 
  2267  ranked based on performance, as augmented by additional points for 
  2268  veterans' preference. Where employees are tied, the employee in the 
  2269  higher tenure subgroup (with subgroup I ranked ahead of subgroup II) 
  2270  will be ranked ahead. When employees are still tied, the employee with 
  2271  the longer service will be ranked ahead.
  2272      In Sec.  351.502 Tenure of employment, OPM is redefining the tenure 
  2273  groups for both the competitive and excepted services. The competitive 
  2274  service tenure group will consist of all competitive service employees
